title.rendered: Blog Post #29: DPS Flat Plan Research

content.rendered:
What Is a DPS Flat Plan?

Purpose

A DPS Flat Plan is a design document used to define the layout of a DPS being made. Designers like to create one before production as it allows them to control, test, and construct the layout before actually placing down elements.

Benefits

Flat plans help organize content by showing the designers where and how to place contents of the DPS. Flat plans are also useful to help build and maintain visual hierarchy, as you can see and imagine the general layout of your DPS without visual clutter. Planning image placement becomes easier since you are free to move around other elements and properly plan to fit in images. Creating flow for readers is ideal with a flat plan since you are able to intelligently pick the best placements of text or images to flow nicely. Using flat plans allows you to avoid design and layout problems down the road as well, as you can control the sizes and positioning of everything before you actually start making your DPS, avoid problems with spacing.

DPS Flat Plan Conventions

  • Visual Hierarchy – The way elements are organized on the DPS. This is important as it determines how elements and text will be seen and read on the DPS. It improves the reader’s experience by clearing organizing elements in a way that’s easy to understand to readers.
  • Modular Design – A design style where certain elements, conventions, fonts, shapes, and general motifs are reused to build visual elements placed on a grid. This is important as it allows designers to more easily keep a consistent, smooth design style that looks good across different elements. This improves the reader’s experience by making the style of the whole magazine consistent, which leaves an impression of professionalism and makes it easy to read.
  • Image Placement – How images are placed and organized on the DPS. This is important as image placement decides how and when readers interpret images. This improves the reader’s experiences by ensuring images are read in the way the author intended, which means readers will understand the article much better and be more immersed in the story.
  • Dominant Image – The main, big image that catches attention. This is important as it catches attention towards the magazine and communicates the tone and style of the magazine. This improves the reader’s experience by giving them a big, appealing, eye-catching image to look at and appreciate, while allowing them to judge the style and tone of the magazine before they decide to read it.
  • White Space – The empty space between margins, images, paragraphs, and other separation objects. This is important as it helps ensure there is enough space to place and read other elements comfortably. This improves the reader’s experience as it makes it easier to read the DPS and gives them space to look around and wander their eyes.
  • Reader Flow – How readers’ eyes move across the page and read the contents of the DPS. This is important as it controls how readers learn and interpret content on the page. This improves the reader’s experience by allowing them to read the DPS in the proper order, keeping textual and visual ideas consistent.

Layout Research

DPS #1

DPS #2

DPS #1 Analysis

For DPS #1, the headline is placed near the middle-left. The image placement is a full-bleed-image paired with a graphic near the top. The body text is in the Columns on the right side, which are used to help organize information. Pull quotes are added near top-left of the DPS. Sidebars are added near the bottom-right. Graphics are placed near the middle-top. The reading pathway starts from the first page top-to-down to the second page that does top-to-down. The image, headline, caption, and graphic work well, but the tiny columns, unaligned image border off the fold, and bottom-placed sidebar don’t work that well, and could be fixed by re-aligning the image border to the fold, giving the columns more space, and placing the sidebar on the sides. The image placement feels particularly intentional, since it acts as a background image for the other elements.

DPS #2 Analysis

For DPS #2, the headline is placed at the very top, spread across the DPS. The image placement is a box for the main image on the left of the magazine. The body text is in the Columns on the right side, which are used to help organize information, along with some small body text boxes on the left. Pull quotes are added near the bottom-right of the DPS. Sidebars are added near the bottom-right. Graphics don’t seem to be specifically planned out. The reading pathway starts from the first page top-to-down to the second page that does top-to-down. The body texts and headline placement work well, but placing the main image as a small box and putting the pull quote at the end of the paragraphs the reader is reading makes the DPS less effective. It could be improved by simply making the main image bigger, adding spaces for graphics, and pull quote and captions near the top-left. The fold-adjacent placement feels intentional, as it shows the designer clearly moved visual elements to account for it.

Dos and Don’ts of DPS Flat Planning

Effective Planning (DO)

  • Use a clear visual hierarchy – Improves the design by ensuring elements look like they were placed in a proper, specific order, making content easier to read and more trustable.
  • Create a strong focal point – Improves the design by giving the reader a main focal point to look at and understand, adding context to the body paragraphs and providing eye-candy/appeal to the DPS.
  • Plan reader navigation – Improves the design by making sure readers look at the context in the proper order you want them to, which allows for better, more concise, and immersive writing.
  • Make important content easy to find – Improves the design by making it easy for readers to find what they want quickly, without interference or difficulty.
  • Balance text and images – Improves the design by ensuring images aren’t too big or text isn’t too big, which gives balance and equal emphasis on both elements of the DPS.
  • Leave sufficient white space – Improves the design by making it easy for reader’s eyes to glance and read the magazine while providing wiggle room for the designer to change or add elements

Poor Planning (DON’T)

  • Ignore alignment – Harms the design by making the DPS difficult to read or process, and gives unprofessional suspects in readers
  • Overlap elements unnecessarily – Harms the design by making it difficult to look at important images or information, giving the reader a hard time.
  • Use too many focal points – Harms the design by making it overstimulating for readers to read and understand, making focal points feel redundant and intrusive.
  • Crowd pages with too much content – Harms the design by making it difficult for both readers and designers to read the page well, and be able to change it freely.
  • Create confusing reader pathways – Harms the design by causing readers become confused and annoyed trying to read the body paragraphs.
  • Use inconsistent layouts – Harms the design by giving unprofessional energy and makes it difficult for the designer to change elements and keep them consistent.

Applying the Research

My DPS Flat Plan Design Rules

  • Images and text will be balanced in size and content.
  • White space will be used to create boundaries between visual elements, but they should not excessively large.
  • Pull quotes will be placed near the top-left.
  • Reader navigation and visual hierarchy should flow naturally.
  • There should be only one strong focal point.
  • Graphics should be around the page to help represent complex topics and add visual appeal.
  • Images should match the surrounding body paragraphs.
  • Fonts and colors should sometimes change briefly to add emphasis, but never for long.
  • Backgrounds should not be dull but have lots of life and patterns behind.
  • Elements should be tightly aligned around each other, and be positioned consistently.

Reflection

I learned that DPS flat plans are made very carefully to guide reader attention, keep visual appeal, and build a sense of professionalism. Dominant image and modular design conventions see to be the most important, as they help build the focal points of magazines and make content feel purposeful and aligned. Designers should avoid planning mistakes like placing elements in places that don’t make any sense, or cause confusing reading flow. I will use big images, organized columns, and pull quote boxes in my own DPS flat plan. This research helps me create a professional magazine by learning how to effectively position, size, and lay out elements on a DPS to preserve visual appeal and communicate ideas.

title.rendered: Blog Post #28: DPS Planning

content.rendered:
Topic and Purpose

The topic of my DPS will cover video game programming and how video games are made on a technical level. I chose this topic since its main headline of my magazine. I want to help communicate the difficulty and thinking required to code games. This is important to my audience since people in my audience are interested in developing video games and want to understand the internal workings on a technical level.

Target Audience

My target audience is teenagers aged 14-18 who are creative and interested in developing, making, and working on video games. They like creative arts like drawing, music production, programming, design, and advertising. My content, covering the technical aspects of game development, paired with a modern, sleek, and exciting design language will appeal and attract my audience well.

Content Plan

  • My working headline will be “The Code Behind Games”.
  • My main article will focus on how developers work on video games: the programming languages, tools, concepts, architectures, and scripts they produce.
  • Key information and research will include quotes from real game developers, architecture explanations from papers, and info from TED talks.
  • I will use infographics, pull quotes, timelines, and fact boxes to support my content.
  • I will include visual diagrams of algorithms and architectures.

Layout Plan

Headline will go near the top of the page. Images will mainly stick to the sides and sometimes be placed around the text, near the middle fold. I will include 3-4 columns in the DPS. I will use minimal amounts of white space, not being super empty, but not packed either. Readers will first see high-level explanations of what game programmers do and then will read analogies and explanations for the lower-level topics. Important information will be bolded or given a specialized visual effect (like a color, font, or style change for 1-2 words).

Visual Design Plan

I will use images and graphics to help add visual appeal and visual representations of the concepts covered in the paragraphs. My color scheme (i. e. black, gray, red, white) will be used to give the magazine a minimalist feel and keep things simple, appealing to my audience by keeping things straight-to-the-point and non-confusing. Fonts and typography will also be used to add importance to important words, stylized text for paragraph introductions, and general visual appeal, which appeals to my audience by adding visual flare and eye candy. Visual style and tone will rely on vibrant, interesting, and complex graphics, making my magazine feel more like a fun activity and less like a newspaper.

Applying What I Learned

I will use magazine conventions like headline placement, white space usage, vibrant graphics, relatable topics, and quotes in my own magazine. DPS #1 in Blog Post #27 inspired me to use vibrant graphics and white space, while a magazine DPS I saw while researching for Blog Post #26 used quotes frequently throughout, inspiring me to also use quotes. I am adapting those magazine conventions and general design tools in my own magazine, as they have been proven to work effectively and been battle-tested across many magazines. I will make sure my own magazine changes its design with these conventions to actually match my content.

Success Criteria

I know my DPS will be successful because I use visual and textual elements (i. e. like technology, coding, retro fonts and references) that pull in and attract my audience. I use modern, minimalist designs in my in visuals, which helps keep my DPS high-quality and appealing to young generations (like my target audience). I will use a discovery-based organization strategy, where convent is revealed in the order the readers discover it while reading. I will use straight-to-the point language and graphics to keep my information clear. I will use tried-and-true magazine conventions adapted to my visual design style to help make my DPS effective.

Reflection

I am excited to make a fun, engaging DPS about my favorite part of game design and programming with vibrant visuals and useful concepts. I anticipate developing high-quality visual elements and good articles will be the most difficult. My analysis and research have influenced many of my choices, including to use common magazine conventions and have vibrant visuals.

Essential Question: How can research and analysis of professional magazine layouts help media producers design an effective and engaging double-page spread?

Research and analysis of professional magazine layouts help media producers design effective and engaging DPSes by showing them what common magazine conventions look like, what works vs. what doesn’t, and giving them inspiration to help them create their own DPS. By looking at other DPSs, they get an idea of what a DPS looks like and what people expect from a DPS, allowing them to formulate layouts and designs with more confidence and clarity. Looking at other DPSes also lets them see what works with audiences, allowing them to copy and adapt strategies into their own DPS.

title.rendered: Blog Post #27: DPS Comparative Analysis

content.rendered:
DPS #1 (Texas Law Magazine, Fall 2024 Issue)

DPS #2 (New Orleans Magazine, “Rise + Shine”)

Publication Info

DPS #1 is from the Texas Law Magazine, while DPS #2 is from the New Orleans Magazine.The articles in DPS #1 discuss student sports, while the article in DPS #2 covers old letters from a city. The target audience for DPS #1 seems to be people interested in laws, sports, AI, and Texas news while the target audience for DPS #2 seems to cover a wider variety of people, specifically those interested in New Orleans’ news and history. DPS #1 seems to be focused on health, policy, and education, while DPS #2 is focused on regional lifestyle.

Convention Analysis

Both DPSes share 5 conventions: Minimal elements, lots of white space, simple fonts, singular striking images, and enlarged font sizes for headlines, captions, or paragraph separators. Both DPSes intentionally use few visual elements in order to reduce confusion design patterns and support a minimalist feel, which affects the audience by making the magazine feel professional and modern. White space is added to the sides of paragraphs, lines, boxes and more to help clearly separate information and provide natural points for the magazine to fold and be held, which impacts the audience by signaling that their experience and readability have been thought after for. Simple fonts are used to make the information clear, familiar, and easily readable, which gives audiences a sense of familiarity (with other magazines they’ve read) and professionalism. Both DPSes use singular images (excluding the advertisement image in DPS #2), which is done to give more impact and intrigue to each image. This impacts the audience and causes to look and process the images more. Enlarged font sizes are used to help separate paragraphs and sections, which helps organize the information and articles. This helps communicate to the audience that the magazine is professional and well-organized.

Layout Comparison

Both look very similar, with almost identical typography, color schemes, balance between text and visuals, and reader navigation. However, the fonts are slightly different and DPS #1 contains more colors, helping it look more interesting. DPS #1 uses images to help build modern graphic design elements, while DPS #2 uses images to give impact/idea on what the article topic is focusing on.

Audience Comparison

DPS #1 appeals to its target audience with quality graphic design elements, relatable stories tied with policy (students), while DPS #2 appeals to its target audience by discussing regional history and lifestyle. The modern graphics design choice in DPS #1 was made to relate to younger generations, who like minimalist and modern designs. DPS #2 uses more simple, bland visual elements and style, which was made to appeal to an older generation/audience, who prefer familiar and clear styles.

Evaluation

I believe DPS #1 is more effective. The vibrant color choice, modern graphics design, and generally relevant topic makes it more attractive and interesting to read than DPS #2. In my own DPS, I will avoid merging ads with my content, using boring-newspaper like fonts, and having bland topics and content. DPS #2 uses ads and has a boring newspaper-like style, making it look unappealing and unattractive to most.

Reflection

I learned what DPSes look like and what makes a DPS look game versus something that looks unappealing. I want to use the color scheming, impactful images, and enlarged fonts for my own magazine DPS. This analysis allowed me to learn what is important towards building a DPS and what works vs. what doesn’t work.

Essential Question: How do different magazines use design conventions to appeal to different audiences and achieve different purposes?

Different magazines use design conventions to help add familiarity & success into their work. By sticking to common conventions, magazines are able to appeal to a wide variety of audiences, and use tried-and-true methods of hooking readers. They can also use conventions to help specifically design their magazines to leave a certain impression on audiences, like bold and unique posing on a fashion magazine going against typical beauty standards, or a travel magazine with submarines or rockets on the cover, exploring new ways and places to travel to.

title.rendered: Blog Post #26: DPS Research

content.rendered:
What is a DPS?

A DPS (Double Page Spread) is two or more adjacent pages next to each other that are combined together make a wider area for text and content. In a magazine, a DPS is used to pack content together and make reading content feel more natural.

Magazine Conventions

Images

Definition: Images in magazines commonly comprise of screenshots, 2d graphics, cinematic imagery, real life photos, scenery, subjects, and/or animals.
Purpose: Images are used in magazines to help add visual and artistic flare, as well as to give a visual representation of the article and text.
Helps Communicate Info to Readers: This helps readers to better understand and visualize the text, especially if the main subject of the text is difficult to describe in words, or if readers aren’t completely comprehending the text.

Color Scheme

Definition: Color schemes in magazines commonly comprise of standard, complementary colors used to color text boxes, graphics, images, borders, or content dividers.
Purpose: They are used to help give the magazine a consistent theme, make appealing imagery, and sometimes invoke specific emotions.
Helps Communicate Info to Readers: This doesn’t necessary communicate specific information to readers, but it makes the magazine feel visually consistent and professional, causing readers to trust and enjoy the content.

Pull Quote

Definition: A quote from an important person, book, or related piece of content.
Purpose: To add credibility or a thoughtful comment to a story.
Helps Communicate Info to Readers: Helps add commentary and expectations to the article/text.

Headline

Definition: Big, flashy text boxes/labels to attract attention
Purpose: Draw readers in and make them excited
Helps Communicate Info to Readers: Helps communicate what the magazine is about and the kind of content it contains to readers

Caption

Definition: Small pieces of text on images or headlines
Purpose: To clarify or add additional context to specific information
Helps Communicate Info to Readers: Helps add context to headlines and pictures

Drop Cap

Definition: Enlarged capital letter at the start of a sentence
Purpose: To indicate where the article starts and add visual flare
Helps Communicate Info to Readers: Makes the start of the articles/paragraphs clear.

Fact Box

Definition: Small box containing facts and bits of information
Purpose: To add extra context, excite readers, and provide information quickly
Helps Communicate Info to Readers: Gives fun or important information quickly

Standfirst

Definition: Small, short introductory paragraph summarizing the magazine content right after the headline
Purpose: To hook readers in
Helps Communicate Info to Readers: To give a quick summary of the article/magazine content, allowing them to get to the information they want quickly

Audience and Purpose

Magazines use different design styles to appeal to different audiences for a variety of reasons. An audience interested in heavy and realistic video games may like a gritty, dark design while mothers taking care of their babies may like a soft, innocent design. Audiences like different things and have different lives, and it’s important to have a design that compliments and reflects their lifestyle and preferences. Layout and design can impact a reader’s view the magazine and how they interpret the information. A minimalist-feel can help support a professional tone, while a more cluttered, packed look can make the reader feel like they are reading an older, 2000s magazine.

Reflection

I believe the images, headlines, and captions are the most important conventions. They are effective because they are the biggest, largest, highest-impact graphics elements inside most magazines. They support the whole vibe, role, and impression of the magazine. I will be relying on these conventions in my own magazine DPS as they are common practice and have been proven to work well and effectively.

Essential Question

How do magazine conventions help communicate information and engage readers?

Magazine conventions help engage readers by using clever tricks and using tried-and-true methods. For example, is a common convention with images to make them graphically distinct with a clever effect or crop, which helps draw attention to the magazine as it is unique and distinct. Headlines are almost always large and made to prioritize the highlights of a story. This tried-and-true method works for attracting readers by hooking them in with the best the magazine has to offer. Magazine conventions also communicate information by packing information into summaries and infographics. Using an article alone is difficult, since readers need to read and understand the full article. By using summaries and infographics, the magazine can communicate that information much quicker and more efficiently.

title.rendered: Blog Post #25: Magazine TOC – Final Submission

content.rendered:
TOC

COVER

Revisions and Improvement

Main revisions I made were to simply just the size and placement of the headlines and sublines in the first and third categories. This readjust makes the headlines feel more professional and ordered. The category ‘Featured Stories’ also got a lot more emphasis thanks to the expanded font and lack of empty space. My peer feedback was the main motivator for this change, as teacher feedback was good. This revisions were necessary to make the TOC look professional and make it look like a final, finished product. These changes made my TOC look like a real magazine TOC and removed dead space.

Audience Effectiveness

My final TOC appeals to my audience in many ways. For starters, my headlines cover topics that appeal to them. For example, I cover game optimization and game coding, which my audience (being attracted to video games and wanting to make their own games), will want to learn more about. My photography also draws them in, since I display real photos of 3D modeling, coding, and level planning. These photos give them a visual idea of what they should expect to see and makes them excited about the displayed stories. The categories draw them in my clearing organizing the information into bunches, which fits the straight-to-the-point, informative type content my audience enjoys. The typography also appeals to them, since it is a retro font. The retro font is a callback to early video games, and is a common style in video games, letting them connect video games to my magazine. Visual hierarchy also helps, since my content is spaced out and ordered professionally, causing them to feel like the magazine is a professional and serious publication.

Application of Research

Research significantly influenced the final product, as it caused me to make a lot of specific design decisions and choices. TOC Research showed me common TOC magazine conventions and ideas for layouts, which helped me formulate my final layout. Audience research taught me that I needed to have minimalist, straight–to–the–point, informative graphics. Flat plan research showed me how designers come up with good looking layouts and where they start to construct their ideas. Professional magazine research showed me how top and well-known magazines look appealing and stand out from the rest; relying on specific styles, bold imagery, and unique graphical designs. Each research session caused me to develop a vague idea of what the TOC would look like in my head, as well as specific design choices that I would make.

Evaluation of the Final Product

I think my greatest strengths are my images and colors. The best design choices were make the Featured Stories box the biggest and to keep the main image entirely on the left page. The TOC guides readers thanks to the simple, 3 vertical category layout, which is familiar to readers, but remains unique by going in descending order instead of ascending order. The TOC also fits the magazine genre since the categories and headlines specifically cover game related content. If I had more time, I would obtain better photos and add a visually unique graphic, like the robot punching through the page in the middle of the TOC.

Reflection

I learned how to design appealing TOCs, use colors, layout, and incorporate feedback. My work evolved from planning to final by starting with flat plans and research, moving up to drafts, getting feedback from students and teachers, and then finally doing refinements to the TOC. The drafting stage was the most difficult since I had to make the magazine under a time limit. The most difficult challenge was figuring out how to lay out my elements. This project made me a stronger media studies student by teaching me how to design well and how to work under time crunches.

title.rendered: Blog Post #24: Critical Reflection on the TOC Peer Review Process

content.rendered:
Evaluating a Peer’s TOC

When reviewing my peer’s TOC, I saw he was making a lifestyle magazine. The magazine was well designed with a clear hierarchy, consistent colors, and consistent fonts. The photography was taken at cars, pools, houses, and other places and looked very professional. The audience was targeted towards people who to build a good career and future for themselves, likely teenagers or young adults. The elements were organized professionally and cleanly, taking advantage of a minimalist design philosophy. The only mistakes I noticed when reviewing his work were small spelling errors and lack of emphasis on the main story.

What You Learned

I while I didn’t pick up any new design ideas or philosophies altogether, I did see how clean layout and good color schemes can really work well to make a good-looking magazine TOC. I will avoid making spelling errors and mistakes like my peer did in my own TOC. This activity showed me how other magazines (including professional ones and my peer’s magazine) like to order their elements, and the quality of the photos they use. This strengthened my understanding of audience expectations by showing me the photo quality, ordered layout, ordering, and general professionalism audiences expect from magazines.

Feedback Given and Received

The most important feedback I gave was to simply just fix a few spelling errors and give the main story more emphasis. The most important feedback I got was to make sure my headlines were bolded and my sublines were not bold. The success criteria told me what to look for when analyzing a magazine cover and where poorly made magazine covers usually lose in clarity or appeal. I think the suggestions about my spacing between headings and my TOC title size were the most useful since they give me advice to improve my TOC’s layout.

Reflection on the Peer Review Process

Outside perspectives are valuable because they can essentially allow you to see your magazine through a new lens; you aren’t limited by your own likes, conventions, or style as you can get a fresh pair of eyes with an unbiased view to look at your magazine’s TOC like how a reader might look at it and get honest feedback on failure points. This feedback helps improve media products by making sure the TOC looks good to readers without obvious problems. Peer review reflects real-world publishing practices as well, since real magazines usually need to go back and forth with multiple teams comprised of different people between multiple departments and partners, meaning that a magazine draft is often changed and refined a lot with a variety of different perspectives before publication. This process helps squeeze out problems and inconsistencies in a magazine TOC that any one person by themselves may not be able to notice.

Revision Plan

I will clean up my layout and sizing of my TOC elements, specifically my headlines, masthead, and sublines. These changes are necessary to make the magazine look more professional and visually consistent, since even tiny margins or errors in spacing can make the magazine feel off. This will naturally improve audience appeal by making my magazine seem like a polished, final, and reliable product rather than a low effort graphic. This makes my magazine more professional since the consistent spacing, clean typography, and clean colors will mimic actual magazines the reader has likely seen before. I really think spacing will have the biggest impact, since that’s my weak point and improving it would make the TOC much easier to read and understand.

Analysis of Media Conventions (CCR #1)

My peer used TOC conventions very well. He placed his elements in a top-to-down format, placing the headline story first with the other category stories to the bottom in an ascending page order. He stuck to consistent spacing, colors, and fonts as well. He placed images next to the relevant content and also added larger images on the second page, just like how real magazines will add large images to entire pages. The only real weakness was that he had a few spelling errors, which breaks the illusion of professionalism and makes the magazine feel less credible.

Audience Evaluation (CCR #2)

My peer targeted his intended audience very well by using catchy headlines, simple typography, and professional-looking photos. The headlines about lifestyle and career help bring in teens and young adults who want to build a stable future and career for themselves. The photography is high quality, so it appeals to readers and makes the magazine feel more credible and polished.

Using Feedback (CCR #3)

The most useful comments were the ones telling me to fix my layout, spacing, and sizing. These comments helped me realize that my inconsistent spacing was noticeable and needed to be fixed. This influenced my revision plans as it told me that I need to fix my layout.

Revision Strategy (CCR #4)

The three main revisions I will do to my TOC are: size changes, position changes, and layout changes. More specifically, I will be reducing the size of my masthead, changing the layout to enhance readability (putting the main category first instead), and repositioning the headlines and sublines to make them feel more consistent and centered. Reducing the size of the masthead helps ensure the magazine’s name doesn’t feel like the main attraction anymore, properly bringing attention to the “Contents” title. Changing the layout simply makes it easier for readers to instantly see the main, headline story quickly. Repositioning the headlines and sublines will make the magazine feel nicer to look at, more organized, and help keep a professional stance and appearance.

Reflection

I learned that TOC design relies on clean consistency across the whole magazine, and that the maintaining professionalism requires good spelling, consistent fonts, consistent colors, and clever layouts. This evaluation is important in media studies since it helps us improve our magazine and get a high-quality final product before the final magazine evaluation. This experience taught me how to critically analyze a magazine TOC for flaws and develop solutions to fix these flaws, allowing me to analyze my own TOCs for flaws and fix them for a overall stronger TOC.

title.rendered: Blog Post #23: TOC First Draft

content.rendered:
MAGAZINE COVER

TOC DPS

Evidence of Application

My flat plan remained largely the same; the layout of the masthead, TOC title, section headers, page numbers, date line and main image remained the same. The only elements that changed were the positioning of the headers, article page numbers, and the size of the section headers. These adjustments were necessary to make the text feel smooth and centered, as well as to allow the text to fit correctly in the boxes.

Critical Creative Reflection

Applying TOC Research

I was inspired by magazine TOCs that put the main image on one side and put the contents on the other. I incorporated the conventions of having the TOC Title and masthead at the top, as well as keeping my page numbers to the bottom to make it easy to locate without difficulty. I adopted layout techniques like hierarchy and left-middle-right splits to help vertically order the elements on the page and order the section headers. These conventions are appropriate for my genre since they are simple and they prioritize minimalism, which is commonly used in magazines to make ordered and clean designs.

Applying Audience Research

My audience expects magazines to cover information in detail and to be very straight-to-the-point. I selected stories about layoffs, game coding, level design, and music because they are crucial to making games, and are essential to understand the gaming industry. I chose a photo of a 3D model cat and wire frame to represent “Industry”, since it signals developers and people working and creating on games, which represents the Industry well. I chose a picture of level design on paper for “Design and Goals”, since it represents someone thinking of the detail, progression, and appearance of a level, which is exactly what design is supposed to be. I chose a picture of computer code for “Featured Stories” since it signals the technical and programming side of games, which is what the stories in “Featured Stories” focus on. This layout appeals to my audience since it’s very simple and minimal, which helps support the “straight-to-the-point” attitude my audience prefers.

Design Decisions

The feature story was placed at the bottom in the biggest box and font. I put the story in the biggest box and font to help draw attention to it. I placed it at the bottom to add a unique factor to my magazine, since most magazines like to set the feature story as the first thing you read, but placing the feature story at the bottom goes against that. I placed the photographs next to my section headers to help represent or visually show the stories inside each section header. I put the pictures on the left side to make it so readers will see them first (humans read left-to-right, so left objects are seen first). This gives readers an idea of what the section header is about before they read the actual stories. I used my categories to help organize all the different stories and topics I wanted to add. This organization not only makes it easy for readers to find what they are looking for (since related information is bunched up together) but it also makes it easier for me to design, since I can make each section header customized to the topics the header covers. I stuck to my pixel-retro like font as it looks more appealing compared to other fonts and remains consistent with my magazine’s typography. I stuck to the color choices I originally used in my mood board to keep consistency and support minimalism. I placed my elements top-to-down vertically, but I placed the location of section headers to be bottom-to-top to make them stand out.

Preparing for Peer Review

I believe I was successful when it comes to maintaining appeal through consistent colors, fonts, and effects. I was successful at following my flat plan and building a quality layout. I am less confident in my exact positioning and images, as some things may be slightly off center by small amounts, and my images may not be the best choices. Text may feel unaligned and boxes may feel too open and empty. I would like my peers to tell me if my images are appealing and if my positioning feels right or off-center/inconsistent. I may need help improving the images to look better, as I’m still learning take good photos.

Reflection

I learned to how effectively design and layout components to make my magazine appealing. I think design choices like the masthead location, TOC title, and page numbers were the easiest since I followed existing conventions to help keep familiarity and mimic professional magazines. Making design choices about the layout and look of my section headers were difficult, though. Trying to order everything right and making sure it looked good was a challenge. My research helped give me ideas for what works well and looks good in a magazine, as well as what my audience would like and prefer. My TOC has developed a lot since the flat plan, since the flat plan’s vision is actually realized now. It maintains similar layout composition while sticking to the style of the main cover.

content.rendered:
Layout Decisions

I placed the masthead and TOC Title at the top to stick to magazine convention and allow readers to quickly identify the pages. I placed the main image on the left side of the image to help give my main image and look appealing. I placed the three section headers on the right side of the page in a down-to-up arrangement, with each header having its own separated block. I did this to help fill up the right side of the page and be unique, as having the elements arranged in the opposite vertical order of reading makes it stand out. I made the bottom header the biggest to add emphasis to the main story inside that header. For Each header, I set a box for the photo and reserved the rest of the header for the headlines, sublines, and page numbers. I arranged the headlines/sublines/page numbers in a vertical order maintain simplicity and make reading the headlines easy. The headers and headlines being organized in a straight vertical order makes reading each headline clear. I want my main image to attract attention first as it will be the largest element in the whole TOC.

Visual Hierarchy

I believe the two most important elements are my main image and first header. They deserve the most space since they are the defining elements of my magazine. The main image is essentially the representative image for my magazine, so it needs to stay prominent and large. The first header needs to be large as well since it contains the main headline story of the whole magazine, so it needs space to provide emphasis to the main headline. Readers will move through the page by first finding the masthead and main image (eyes will naturally be placed at the top left because of human tendency to start reading something by the top left), and then readers will look down and find themselves at the header sections, and because they are organized in a straight vertical line, readers will naturally read their way down into the headers. They will read the final header (Header #1) last, keeping the main story and headlines fresh in their mind.

Audience Appeal

My target audience are teenagers 14-18 who have creative talents and are interested in game development. This layout appeals to them because it provides space for me to show them a variety of game development topics, which will naturally pull in their interest. My game development main image being prominent and large will naturally appeal to their interests and catch their attention. I decided to make my TOC very straightforward and non-cluttered because when I was conducting audience research, a lot of my interviewees said they like minimalist and straight-to-point content instead of flashy or cluttered content.

Research Connections

In my previous blog post, Flat Plan #2 inspired me the most since it was a functional DPS (double page spread) and it put the main image on the entire left page, giving it lots of space to look good while being easy to read. I borrowed the 3 article-header blocks and the main image placement from the Flat Plan. My research told me to avoid cluttered and packed TOCs (like Flat Plan #3 from the previous blog post).

Reflection

During the planning process, I learned how to clearly organize magazine elements in a clean and appealing way. I think putting the main image on the left side of the page was the easiest, as I really liked it from my research. Figuring out where to place the masthead and TOC Title were the hardest choices since I don’t know the best orientation or size to give to them (during my research I found a variety of different placements). Audience research influenced my choices by making me choose to make a minimalist, simple TOC layout instead of packing a lot of different elements together. TOC Research strengthened my design by giving me good ideas of what has worked in the past and what conventions designers use. This flat plan will give me the proper blueprint to help structure my TOC well and make it look good when I begin making it.

They fit my magazine genre (game development magazine) by explaining how games are made and the relevant industry around them. My audience, if they want to be informed about gaming or work in the industry, would want to learn about the design processes behind their favorite games.

Categories

I created each category to help group the general topic of each story together to help organize everything I wanted to say. These categories help readers go to the topic they are most interested about without needing to flip through the pages to find what they want. These categories are appropriate for my genre as well since they discuss game development.

DPS Selection

My “The Code Behind Games” headline ended becoming up my main DPS. It is the most important story since it covers the most central part of game development (i. e. programming and coding). title.rendered: Blog Post #19: Analyzing Magazine TOCs

content.rendered:
Edge Magazine 2021 Issue 358 (TOC #1)

Game Player’s Magazine 1989 Issue 1 (TOC 2)

First Impressions

TOC #1

The first thing the eyes are drawn to is the large “Table of Contents” header, as it is in a large font and is placed at the top-left of the image, which is where are eyes are naturally drawn to when reading text in an image or paragraph. I think the designer wanted to make it clear what the TOC page was supposed to be and to help communicate to readers where to find the stories they want to read. The second and third things I notice are the two tall images on the right of the page for the Deathloop interview and “Apex Legend’s Newest Reveal”. This design guides readers through the page by first putting their eye at the top left, and moving down to all the stories, moving to the right of the page as each story gets a progressively taller image. This visual hierarchy is effective because it guides the reader through the image smoothly whilst informing them of all the relevant stories.

TOC #2

The first thing my eyes are drawn to are the images at the top, which contain game screenshots and retro art. I think the designer wanted to catch reader’s attention with real video games, making the magazine feel more fun and connected to their interests. The second and third things I notice are the large purple “CONTENTS” text spanning vertically on the left side of the page and the two large transparent green and yellow squares in the background. The design guides readers through the page, first starting at the top with all the images and “CONTENT” caption, then moving down to the list of stories in the magazine. This visual hierarchy is less effective since it feels a lot more cluttered and less visually organized, with inconsistent patterns with the arrangement of elements.

Evaluating Design Decisions

Layout and Organization (TOC #1)

I think the designer intentionally organized the page in a left-to-right manner to help easily guide readers through the table of contents and to remain modern-looking. This layout helps readers find information quickly since it’s all concentrated to path of the eyes looking at the image. The slowly increasing height of the images and minimalistic style (less colors and fonts) are by far the most effective, as they create a natural path for the eyes to follow and stops the magazine from feeling old or unofficial. Although, some could argue that is it a little too minimalistic, so adding more visual elements organized in the right ways could significantly improve the perception of the TOC. The overall layout is successful at correctly communicating to readers all the relevant stories and how to find them without looking poor or odd to look at.

Layout and Organization (TOC #2)

I think the designer intentionally organized the page in a simple, book-style manner is to help make the magazine feel familiar and easy-to-read. The list-like layout is much simpler and recognizable than other magazines, sticking to graphic-book like conventions. This layout helps readers find info quickly by reusing a format they are already accustomed to and not making them use more mental effort to understand a visually complex TOC. The simple list and images at the top are the best aspects, as they are easy-to-understand and hook readers in. Aspects like the color choice, visual element count, and caption placement could be changed to look more modern and better flow with the eyes, like cutting out small subline texts, removing background grid and objects, transforming the Contents caption to be at the top-left of the image, and more. The layout is overall successful at communicating to readers where all the magazine articles are but could be improved with better color and visual element choice.

Images (TOC #1)

I believe the images in TOC #1 were chosen because each image was the corresponding image to one of the magazine stories. The images support the magazine’s genre by hinting to readers/onlookers that the magazine has video games inside it, which logically leads to the magazine’s genre being video games. The images also appeal to the target audience by showing the audience games and characters they like. The image on the right is the most effective since it is the tallest image in the TOC, and thus has the most emphasis and power. The images don’t communicate any specific message; instead, they help add context, appeal, and recognizability to each of the magazine stories.

Images (TOC #2)

I believe the images in TOC #2 were chosen to help add appeal and excite readers with the games they might see inside the magazine. The images support the magazine’s genre and appeals to the target audience by showing genre-appropriate imagery and giving readers an idea of what some of the games look like. There is no particularly effective or focus image, instead there is a grid of 4 images with varying sizes and positions. The images help communicate what the featured games will look like to help readers get an idea of what they’re about to see.

Typography (TOC #1)

The fonts on TOC #1 were chosen to help maintain minimalism and consistency with the basic color scheme and lack of visual elements. These fonts help reinforce the magazine’s identity as a informational and straight-to-the-point magazine by not causing visual clutter. This contributes to the overall tone as a neutral and minimal magazine. The typography choice to switch to a more stylized font for the story sublines help add a bit of style and flare to a dull image to make it still look nice, even with less visual elements. I would also make the table of contents have more unique typography as well to add visual flare.

Typography (TOC #2)

The fonts on TOC #2 were chosen to help keep simplicity. The whole TOC only uses 1 font, just with different colors. This helps reinforce the magazine’s identity and tone as simple and book-like. No particular typography choices are used to help enhance the TOC or add visual flare. I would definitely change some of the fonts to be more unique and stylistic to help add appeal for readers.

Colors and Design (TOC #1)

The colors (being black, white, and yellow) help support the magazine’s genre and objective as a minimalist and informative magazine with no visual clutter or fluff. These colors naturally appeal to the audience since they establish a design consistency framework for the rest of the magazine, keeping an appealing design throughout the magazine. No specific emotions are ideas are communicated via the colors, they were chosen to be simple and easily keep consistency throughout the magazine. The color scheme is very successful as it establishes an appealing design framework throughout the magazine that is easy for the designer to stick to.

Colors and Design (TOC #2)

The colors (being white, purple, yellow, black, and green) support the magazine’s genre and objective with a variety of colors for varied visual elements, reflecting the wide variety of games the magazine covers. These colors appeal to the audience by adding lots of visual content and real imagery to see. The colors don’t invoke any special or emotional feelings, the colors were selected to help add lots of visual elements. The color scheme works but could be improved with more complementary colors and better color arrangement.

Audience and Effectiveness

TOC #1

The target audience is people who are interested in the latest game releases and what people think of them. This is evident because TOC #1 has a lot of game reviews and has a few special stories like interviews, which shows they are trying to appeal to people who want opinions on a variety of games. The TOC appeals to this audience by clearly showing them where all the reviews are located and putting a large chunk of the review in succession, so readers don’t need to skip around the magazine too much to read each review. The TOC is successful in meeting the needs of its audience by clearly arranging and showing the reviews to be convenient for readers.

TOC #2

The target audience is kids, teenagers, or young adults who want to learn about all the different spheres and communities of gaming. This is evident by the fact that the magazine covers a lot of gaming platform groups, with few stories outside of talking about gaming platform groups. The TOC appeals to this audience by giving them lots of examples and explanations on what these other gamers on other platforms do to play games, covering the advantages and disadvantages of each platform. The TOC is overall successful as it covers a wide variety of gaming-related topics, informing its target audience about the gaming world.

Comparing the two TOCs

I think TOC #1 has the strongest layout overall, as it looks a lot more stylistically consistent and modern than TOC #2. TOC #1 wins in color scheme as it uses high-contrast, clean colors vs. TOC #2 which has a lot more confusing, less clean colors. TOC #2 is easier to navigate thanks to it using a familiar book-like layout, whilst TOC #1 uses a more confusing left-to-right layout, but this is a minor win for TOC #2. TOC #1 has a much better use of images as well, as the images look like they actually match the discussed stories, vs TOC #2 which has 4, almost random feeling images at the top that don’t seem to support a specific purpose. TOC #1 has a more appealing visual hierarchy as well, as it uses a unique and clear left-to-right arrangement while TOC #2 has a more book-styled up-to-down arrangement. TOC #1 is just more appealing to the audience because it looks cleaner and is arranged in a unique way (i. e. cleaner colors, unique left-to-right arrangement).

Design Decisions for my own TOC

Design Choices I Will Use

I plan to include the simplicity of TOC #1’s colors, fonts, and left-to-right placement in my own TOC. I believe these features are effective because they keep appeal whilst making design easier for me. TOC #1 mainly inspired all of these changes.

Design Choices I Will Avoid

TOC #2’s design choices to use a familiar book style and more color variety makes the magazine feel less unique and less clean. They do not work well because they are boring and conflicting to readers. I will avoid these mistakes by sticking to a simple 3 color schema and always maintaining a minimalist style.

Research-Informed Decisions

I plan to include a 3-color scheme because it effectively helped readers to learn the magazine’s design style quickly and add a level of recognizability to my magazine. I will avoid using lots of colors because it made TOC #2 less effective by looking more confusing, random, and unclean. My audience research suggests that I should stick to a few fonts and cut down on visual flare because my research indicated people like more straight-to-the-point content.

Reflection

The most effective TOC feature I encountered was the left-to-right contents arrangement of TOC #1. The least effective one was the varied color scheme of TOC #2. This activity helped me understand magazine design a lot more by analyzing what makes a magazine look good or bad. This analysis taught me valuable skills and conventions to use when designing my own TOC. Evaluating media products before before making your own media product is important since you can learn a lot from what has worked in the past vs. what has failed in the past.

content.rendered:
Edge Magazine 2021 Issue 358

Game Player’s Magazine 1989 Issue 1

Analysis (Edge Magazine)

Layout and Organization

In Edge Magazine’s TOC, each story is organized side-to-side. The layout is simple, just using a few bits of text and images. The TOC guides readers by putting the most relevant stories first and giving the required page numbers to see what’s next and what’s available. The large text with small captions and big images makes it simple and easy to navigate.

Visual Design

Basic colors like yellow, black, and white are used. The only images on the TOC are the sub cover images for each of the stories, cropped to fit on the page better. The images are arranged alongside the page numbers and titles. The text has lots of vertical space but short horizontal space due to the tight crops of the images.

Typography

A bold, large, simple letter font is used for the page numbers and headings. This typography gives the magazine a simple, straightforward, minimalist mood. The “Table of Contents” caption as the top and rightmost image stand out the most. The rightmost image stands out because it has the largest heading and image, and the Table Of Contents caption stands out as well because it uses the largest font on the page and is at the very top left, which is naturally where are eyes are primed to begin reading something.

Content Selection

The featured stories are mainly about game reviews, interviews, and coverage of certain games. The right most story (“DEATHLOOP CREATORS EXCLUSIVE INTERVIEW”) naturally seems to be very important because it is the tallest image. The second and third most important-appearing stories are a game review (“DISCO ELYSIUM: THE FINAL CUT”) and a simple coverage story of another game. (“APEX LEGEND’S NEWEST REVEAL”). These stories look important as well since they are the second/third tallest images in the TOC.

Audience and Purpose

The target audience clearly seems to be towards teenagers and adults interested in a wide variety of game releases and genres. The TOC appeals to that audience by providing a varied selection of interviews, reviews, and coverage of games. The minimalist and simple feel helps it feel like a modern technology magazine and sets up the design consistency pattern for future pages.

Analysis (Game Player’s Magazine)

Layout and Organization

The information is organized in a similar list manner, going down. The layout is a bit more complex with multiple shapes in the background, graphics images at the top, and a rotated “CONTENTS” caption. The TOC easily guides readers with its familiar list pattern, showing all the page numbers for all the relevant stories. The simple font and text on the list makes it easy to navigate.

Visual Design

Yellow, green, purple, and yellowed-white are used on the TOC. Retro games and art also appear. The images are tiled/bunched together near the top. Both the text and the images take up the two vertical halves of the image, which means both have lots of space to work with. The bottom vertical half is for the text, and the top vertical half is for the images.

Typography

Simple, basic, and bold fonts are used for both the page numbers and headings. This typography helps keep the magazine more straight-to-the point and informational rather than attempting to push a mood or narrative. The large text of “CONTENTS” stands out the most because it uses a different color (purple) and is rotated to the left-side, giving the other elements spacing and catching the eye via left-to-right reading.

Content Selection

Stories about consoles, specific game titles, and game publishers are included. The very last title feels the most important since it is the longest and includes a famous, well-known game called “Super Mario Bros”. The magazine seems to want readers to view the middle sections of the magazine, as that’s where the most packed stories are. I can tell because every single title in the middle (stretching to the first few small titles and ending at the final very long title) is almost equal length, clearly showing how the middle is the “meat” of the magazine.

Audience and Purpose

The target audience seems to be young kids and teenagers looking at game consoles and games to play. The TOC appeals to that audience by covering stories about different types of consoles and players, opinion pieces, general game coverage, and a review of the massively popular title “Super Mario Bros”. The design reflects the magazine’s genre as well. By using grids, shapes, and video game imagery, it clearly communicates the magazine’s purpose as a video game magazine alongside clean graphics.

Comparison

The designs share quite a few differences and similarities. Both designs only use a handful of colors, stick to a minimalist font or style, have a large bold TOC caption, and include video game imagery. The main differences is that Edge Magazine sticks to minimalism better by using high-contrast colors while Game Player’s Magazine uses more old school, blendable colors. The TOCs also talk about games from different time periods, with Game Player’s Magazine talking about older consoles (like the Atari, NES, and Amiga) whilst Edge Magazine talks about modern titles like Monster Hunter and Apex Legends. I believe Edge is more effective as it looks more unique with its horizontally arranged stores, has better minimalist colors, and covers modern games and topics vs Game Player’s Magazine TOC which uses older color schemes, old consoles, and more generic organization. I plan to use some of the minimalist style and corresponding images style that Edge Magazine uses in my own TOC.

Applying My Research

In my own TOC, I will include a large caption, simple/bold font, red/white/black color scheme, and images relevant to each story. I will use 3-4 images to represent the stories. I will organize page titles by every 2 pages and use article titles similar to the cover’s headlines. TOC Design conventions like a large TOC caption, simple background, and images appear most often in the two TOC’s I analyzed. I will use minimalism to my advantage to help make my magazine professional; minimalism allows you to build good looking designs without complex or difficult-to-design visual elements. I will avoid using odd color schemes, and cropped images in my own TOC.

Reflection

Magazine TOCs surprised me with the fact that many of them are overly simple and lack extreme visual cluttering. This research taught me that gaming magazines like to stick to minimalism and various conventions like large TOC captions. Researching existing media products before creating your own is important since you can learn a lot of important information on the best ways to design your magazine, and learn how to avoid common mistakes as well. This research showed me common mistakes to avoid and good style formats to use to help me create a better looking magazine.

title.rendered: Blog Post #17: Magazine Cover – Final Edition

content.rendered:
Final Cover

Revision and Improvement

Throughout the design process, I added lots of graphics and made a lot of design choices. After the draft, I made a few key changes: changing the main image, reducing the subline size, adding an outline to the font, and removing the black text boxes. The feedback about my sublines being too long is what made me to significantly shorten them down. I also got feedback that my main image had conflicting colors with my headlines, so I changed the main image to reduce clutter and color variety. I think the removal of the boxes and change of the main image boosted the quality by a large margin. Going through multiple revisions of changing various elements of my cover allowed me to slowly improve on certain aspects one by one, building up to my final cover.

Design Decisions

I selected the robot image as my main cover image because it has a subject (so I can take advantage of direct address), but it also has code and planning paper in the background, which helps clearly communicate the magazine’s genre as a game design magazine and capture my audience by enticing them with game design related concepts. This image also helps support my main story (“The Code Behind Games”) as it shows code and planning paper, hinting to the game design process that I will discuss in the magazine. The color scheme of red, white, and black is appropriate for my genre since it is a simple color scheme that is readable, appealing, and has had much success with other magazine publishers like Game Developer or PC Gamer. The font choices of retro fonts combined with newspaper/magazine fonts (commonly used by other publications, Times New Roman, Maragsa, etc.) help communicate the style/purpose of my magazine (game design, behind-the-scenes) whilst sticking to magazine conventions that other genres also take advantage of. The layout is clear as it attracts attention via the main image and masthead and slowly guides readers down the image with descending headlines, eventually landing to the main story at the bottom.

Audience and Effectiveness

My target audience is teenagers aged 14-18 who are interested in game design and have creative talents. My cover attracts my audience by clearly showing off as a game design magazine via my main image’s subject (the 3D game robot), using retro fonts, and having code in the background. These features are appealing to my audience and hook them in because they discuss common topics they know about or want to know about, use colors they recognize from other similar publications, and use recognizable font styles (retro arcade) to communicate their genre and provide a callback to older video games. My magazine wins over other game design magazines because it covers a wide variety of topics and looks stylistically consistent with similar colors, fonts, and text across the page.

Reflection on the Production Process

The most challenging part of the design process was making the main image. Trying to quickly make a quality image that works with my magazine design and theme was difficult, and I experimented with a variety of lighting conditions, subjects, and ideas for the framing of the main image. I learned how to create quality renders, how to make text look exciting and not bland, and how to place visual elements effectively. I learned that magazine design relies on conventions and clear text to work effectively, as lower-quality work that strays from conventions often turn into a poster. The planning, revisions, and peer-review significantly helped me through the design process by guiding me what to change, add, or remove next to keep improving and advancing my magazine’s design. If I had more time, I would probably try to get a better camera shot with good lighting, high-quality characters, and better communication of the magazine’s genre.

Reflecting on My Progress

I think I improved on three main skills with this project: how to make visually appealing images, how to work and write under pressure, and how to turn feedback into improvement. I learned to make visually appealing images by carefully aiming and testing different settings when creating my main image, like lighting, resolution, framing, and more. The tight deadlines allowed me to find ways to work even under a time crunch to create quality products, like managing time and working on assignments during free time at school. I had to learn how to take feedback from my peers and instructors and turn that into change to improve my magazine cover, like shortening down my sentences and changing my main image.

title.rendered: Blog Post #16: Critical Reflection on the Peer Review Process (Magazine Cover)

content.rendered:
I peer-reviewed my peer’s magazine cover, who was making a women’s sports magazine. The target audience seemed to be comprised of people who enjoy sports and improving equality in sports, like women, transgender people, and minority groups. The magazine had most of the required conventions, like mastheads, headlines, sublines, and a main image. I believe the wording of the headlines was the most effective as they clearly communicated the magazine’s purpose, as well as covering interesting topics. The layout was not close to professional magazine standards as a good majority of the headlines were bunched near the top and lacked visual flare. The main image (a slightly blurred image of a line of athletic women in a sporting court) looked fine but felt weak as it didn’t contain a proper subject, central idea, or clear purpose. The headline text was very good and properly built excitement but the lack of visual appeal or ordered placement makes them feel boring and weak for the target audience. The font was good as it used a stylistic font but failed to use color variety as the only colors I found were white and blue, which are very monotone and standard.

I was able to learn how to avoid common design mistakes and pitfalls by peer-reviewing another’s magazine cover, as well as how to improve my main image. The main mistakes I saw were lack of correct placements, lack of subject in main image, and lack of stylistic appeal. By evaluating my peer’s cover, it better taught me what exactly are the do’s and do not’s of the magazine cover design process. My peer’s main image does use warmer colors and background blur to help make a more readable image, which is something I could learn from to help decrease the sharper colors in my own cover. This activity taught me that magazine conventions are used to help make covers look good, and straying from those conventions must be done carefully and wisely in order to maintain appeal.

I gave my peer some feedback to help them improve their magazine cover. For example, I told them to shorten down their headlines as some of them were too long. I told them to use a subject in their main image. I supported these comments by reviewing the guidelines provided to us on the main feedback sheet, i.e. headlines shouldn’t be more than 4-5 words, main image should be visually interested, etc. I received some feedback on my own magazine cover as well, mainly that my magazine had excessively long headlines. When designing my final cover, I will shorten down my headlines and sublines by a large amount, making each headline/subline a few words long. I will also improve my main image to be less conflicting with my color scheme. These changes will significantly improve the readability of my magazine cover, attracting more of my target audience to read my magazine.

Receiving feedback from others is important as it helps improve and grow our design skills. Peer review helps the designer notice strengths and weaknesses they may have not noticed before by letting someone else with a fresh perspective view the magazine cover without bias. This means that issues, bias, or tiny details that the designer might have glossed over can be picked up by a fresh pair of eyes that don’t have any connection to the cover. By patching up weak points and reviewing feedback, the magazine cover becomes more appealing and structured in general, which will naturally improve appeal to the target audience. The peer review process simulates real magazine via double review. In real magazine creation, a review team will review and edit a magazine to make it suitable for publication, sending the magazine back to the design team if major changes need to be made. Peer review is similar in the sense that another person will review your magazine cover for weaknesses and report suggestions to improve.

This activity developed my ability to understand design choices, critique designs effectively, and audiences. By analyzing my peer’s cover, I was able to go through the image and imagine how they chose to place and structure visual elements. I also learned how to identify weaknesses in a design and how to give effective feedback to improve the design. I also learned how to identify main ideas and audiences to better fit and understand the magazine cover around the target audience.

title.rendered: Blog Post #13: Magazine Cover Flat Plan Research & Analysis

content.rendered:
I selected to make a game development magazine. I chose this genre because it is a genre that I am very knowledgeable about and that I am passionate about myself. I make games and work with others in my free time, so designing a magazine about game design helps me understand the game design industry better and share my talent with others. However, I need to attract readers of my genre first in order to share any information at all, and thus I will need to design a flatplan for the main cover. I hope that analyzing flatplans will help me learn how to structure an image to capture attention while also keeping the magazine’s topic clear.

Flat Plan A

Flat Plan A has the masthead and skyline at the top, which help provide even spacing and clearly communicate the magazine brand. The main cover line and subheading help attract readers with a shocking fast or big story, hooking them in. The bubble helps provide extra information to the contents in the magazine and also helps add additional headlines. The main image is the majority section of the magazine; it’s the stylistic image that attracts the eye first and gets readers excited. The coverlines boxes show additional, secondary headlines that are less important. The web address box is there to show to users that the magazine has an online web presence, allowing them to further get invested in the magazine brand. The bottom Date/Issue, Price, and Barcode boxes are there to help readers and shops identify the magazine, as well as to clearly communicate the magazine’s selling price.

Flat Plan B

Flat Plan B is similar to Flat Plan A, but it has a few key changes that separate it. Just like Flat Plan A, Flat Plan B also has a main image and masthead to help hook readers in and communicate the magazine brand. However, this time, many of the headline boxes and captions are placed on the left and right sides. The feature captions help tell readers what’s in the magazine and what topics are discussed. The small image captions help add more images to the cover, potentially hooking readers even more with related subtopics. These 2 caption types are spread across the sides, making the magazine look appealing and interesting all throughout the cover.

Flat Plan C

Flat Plan C is nearly identical to Flat Plan A with only a few minor differences. Once again, the masthead, skyline, main image, barcodes, price, issue, and date are visible. The masthead/skyline helps clearly show the brand and give some spacing or headroom, main image draws in attention and emphasis, and barcodes/issue/price help readers make an informed purchase and correctly identify the magazines. This time, however, the date and price are moved to the top to reduce distraction and keep uniformity with magazine conventions. The bubble has been replaced with a Splash box, which does the same thing (help add additional, big headlines) just with a unique shape and different placement to better attract attention. The smaller coverline boxes have been replaced with one big box taking up a large chunk of the right side called the “Sell Lines”. This box serves the same purpose (adding additional less important headlines), but it does so in a more organized, clean way that allows readers to skip over it if they wish.

These three cover flat plans have many similarities and differences. They all usually contain a masthead, main image, and places to add extra headlines or content. However, Flat Plan B lacks a skyline and an area to add a price, date, or issue number. Every flat plan places the headline boxes to different sides of the image. Flat Plan B is the most visually effective, since it allows the subject to be framed in center with other useful and attractive elements placed to the sides. Flat Plan B also best represents the gaming genre since it allows all the different components of the game development process to be included on one page. The design choices of focus on main image and masthead at the top dominate in all 3 of these flat plans.

Overall, Flat Plan B inspired me the most as it shows how I can fit a lot of game development aspects on the front cover. In my own flat plan, I will include the masthead, skyline, main image, feature captions, and small image captions. This research will allow me to learn what works when designing magazines and how to build attractive cover images. I may face challenges like trying to make well designed graphics, visual composition, or lack of variety.

The camera shot is a medium shot at eye-level angle with direct address, meaning the subject is centered first. This image instantly attracts attention by using its bold stance and clear camera framing to create an emotional idea: this game is real, epic, and serious. This helps support the magazine’s purpose as a in-depth review of Battlefield 3 by making readers excited before they begin reading.

The magazine features many mini-headlines covering many different but related topics. Certain game releases, gaming technology, and How-2-Play guides are included. Words are emphasized via bolding and flashy tags like “KILLER HORROR” or “MASSIVE REVIEW!”. Many emotional and attention grabbing words-and-phrases like “Zombies in Bikinis!”, “How to Save Adventure Games”, “Amazing Tech”, “The Saviour of Shooters” are used to help attract attention to the magazine and its many subtopics. These headlines suggest that the magazine likes to generally focus on game releases, gaming technology, and potentially other gaming-related subtopics.

Captialized, bolded, modern fonts are used. The typography helps reinforce the game’s dark-and-gritty theme by not adding silly or humorous letters. Red, whire, and black dominate the color scheme, which help make the magazine feel minimalist and modern. This targets a gaming audience who like new, bold, and appealing visual styles. The most noticeable items are the game character and game title. The eye naturally is drawn towards the center, specifically on the character. Less important headers and titles are pushed to the side whilst the main focus of the magazine (the subject, masthand, and brand title) are pushed to the center and top. This helps guide the reader’s attention by first hooking them in with a large and flashy subject, and then leading them around the image to all the mini-headlines.

The intended reader seems to be gamers specifically invested in the shooter game genre. I can infer this from the fact that this magazine says Battlefield 3 is “the saviour of shooters”, implying the reader is bored or unsatisified with existing shooters, which means they likely play video games. They are likely interested in playing shooter games often and being highly competitive with friends or online players. They are most likely male since the dark-and-gritty tone tend to lean more towards being a male quality in our society. The purpose of the magazine seems to inform and entertain, as they reference reviews and flashy graphics. The magazine invokes excitement and seriousness.

This cover is good at attracting attention by using it’s bold title and subject. It clearly communicates the genre by mentioning “Gamer”, shooters, and top-game IP like Battlefield. It appeals to the audience by focusing on minimalism and cool features. Direct address and medium shot as photography choices help frame the subject well.
