title.rendered: Blog Post #10 – Camera Shots and Angles : Research

content.rendered:
There are 6 different camera angles and shots commonly used in magazines. They are High Angle, Bird’s Eye View, extreme close ups, Eye level angle, long shots, and medium shots.

High Angle is when the shots are taken above, looking down at a subject. Photographers may choose this angle because they want to make something feel inferior or smaller than something else, as if they are something to be looked down upon. This communicates inferiority and tiny sizes compared to a larger force. It could cause fear or awe in the audience depending on the character or subject the shot is focused on. A magazine may use this as a cover image or to place focus on an object. This may appeal to an audience who like contrasting powers or forces fighting.

Bird’s Eye View are similar to High Angle, but the angle looks straight down more. Photographers may use this angle because they want to give a complete image of a scene or add emphasis on a large object in the frame. It helps communicate the scene’s full context or subject without much cropping. It gives a wide space to show small details on its subjects. A magazine may use this to create a cover image or give full information on a scene or object. This may appeal to an audience who like stylistic, full shots of food and nature.

Extreme close ups are when shots are taken very close to the subject. This helps add extra emphasis on the subject and communicates small details from the subject. This will likely cause fear or surprise in the audience since this shot is usually used to emphasize an important detail or add suspense to the scene. A magazine may use this for cover images or to build certain emotions in an image. This may appeal to a audience who enjoys movies or dramatic photos.

Eye Level Angle is when the shots are taken at eye level, looking straight ahead towards a subject. Photographers may choose this angle because they want to directly address a subject without invoking any specific feelings. This better communicates other objects or characters in the scene without impact from the camera angle. It could cause no specific feeling or observation in the audience depending on the character or subject the shot is focused on. A magazine may use this to give a direct, general idea on an object and instead use the scene to give the shot meaning. This will likely appeal to an audience who like faces or makeup.

Long shots are when shots are taken with a wide field of view with a subject and surrounding environment. Photographers may choose this angle to help communicate the environment around a certain lifestyle or person. This communicates not just the subject, but their world view and ideas. It makes the subject appear small yet significant. This may cause awe in the audience as this angle is commonly paired with vast scenes. It is most effective when you need to add contrast to a small or big subject. Magazines may use this to give contrast between opposing forces or subjects. This appeals to an audience who may enjoy large contrast, and how small forces can still take on large forces.

Medium shots are when shots of a subject are taken waist to head up. Photographers usually choose this to photograph people, as it gives the person full emphasis, makes them look approachable, and provides space for other elements. This helps communicate what the subject looks like clearly while maintaining readability. This usually causes interest in the audience as people are tempted to read the magazine to learn more about the subject. It is most effective when it shows people. Magazines usually use this for cover images or to represent certain people. This may appeal to an audience interested in celebrities and celebrity drama.

Medium, Long, and Eye Level shots help show authority by adding focus on a subject or showing an environment based around a subject. Extreme close ups help build closeness to the audience by giving detailed information about character expressions and thoughts. To attract teens, Medium and Eye Level shots are ideal since they give good emphasis on attractive subjects. On professional magazine covers, Bird’s eye view, Long, and Medium shots dominate. Professionals use these because they often look very visually appealing and provide good emphasis on a subject or environment. For example, a food magazine I found (Fine Cooking), used a Bird’s Eye View shot on food.

My Photography Plan

For my magazine cover, I plan to use an extreme close up. I will use Eye Level shots, Bird’s Eye View, and High Angle Shots. These are the best choices for my audience since they show the game design process in detail. My audience is mainly comprised of talented teens 14-18, with skills like music, art, and coding. They will naturally want to see the finer details of the game development process, so using close-up shots combined with angles that prioritize readability and looks. This will help me communicate my genre and purpose by making game development an obvious and easily readable element of my magazine.

CCR Connection

Understanding camera shots and angles allows me to better understand how to frame subjects in a photo to communicate a purpose. It allows me to produce photos like other magazines of game design. When I understand camera shots, it makes copying shots and ideas a lot easier. Understanding how camera shots give meaning helps me better curate my images to my audience by giving detailed close-up shots.

title.rendered: Blog Post #7: Audience Research & Target Audience

content.rendered:
My media product is a Gaming Magazine. I will be covering the development of video games and how modern games are produced. It’s important to understand my audience in order to figure out the best ways to design my graphics and structuring to appeal to my main audience.

For my research, I decided to ask school students at the local eSports club at my school who were playing games. I was able to ask 23 people in total, most of them ranging 14-18 years old. I chose these people mainly because they represent my audience very well. My audience is teens and young adults interested in gaming, so high schoolers who go to the eSports club will naturally have those qualities.

The research was quite informative. The 5 questions I asked them were: “How often do you consume media about gaming, whether it be through videos or articles?”, “Do you actually enjoy video games often?”, “Do you prefer informative media, or flashy stylized media?”, “What are the most popular games you play?”, and “What other hobbies do you enjoy outside of gaming?”. The 3 most important things I found were that: people prefer more informative pieces of content than hyper-stylized ones, many people had general interests in working on computers, art, and music, and people usually prefer lesser-known indie game titles over big studio projects. About 13 of them did mention interest in making in their game projects, as you can see in one of the interviews:

“Me: Okay, the next question is: Do you have any interests outside of gaming? So, like, do you have anything cool you do outside of gaming? Subject: I like to draw a lot. That’s one of my strong suits. I kinda wanna work on game art, I actually drew some of my OCs for a game idea I had in my mind.” (Context: OCs is short for “original characters”).

These findings are important since they show that people prefer more straight-to-the-point magazines, and how game development is a big share of these people’s interests and skill set. This shows how there is a big potential audience who may want to read my magazine, as we can easily imagine how these 13 people could turn into a large group over millions of gamers.

My target audience is going to be aged around 14-18, which includes teens and young adults interested in gaming. Their interests will include gaming, art, music, coding, and production. They will enjoy indie games and be around middle to college level in education. They will enjoy playing games, watching behind-the-scenes footage, idea and design sketching, and the creation of game assets.

I chose this audience because it’s the ideal audience according to my research. Gaming is an activity most commonly practiced by teens and young adults (ages 18-34 make up 38% of all gamers according to inStreamly, with people under 18 also making up 20% according to the same source), so this research shows how there is a large market who would be interested in my game development magazine (13 / 23 potential interests). People who enjoy art, music, or coding will also likely enjoy my magazine.

My audience mainly needs information to learn and be informed. Because they focus on game development, they need info on how the game production pipeline works and how they might fit in this pipeline. My magazine will explain how games are made and each role that participates in the development of a game, offering these people valuable information about how they can use their own skills to support this pipeline or start it themselves.

I believe Gauntlett’s Identity Theory will help me explain my audience. My audience is interested in creative work, like arts & music. They will naturally want to express themselves by creating creative products like video games. They may use the information I give to base their identity and learning around it, so they can get a better chance for a job at a game studio and be the ideal worker.

My target audience includes people ages 14-18 who are interested in game development with creative talents like art, music, or coding. Probably the most important things I learned are that my magazine needs to prioritize information and usefulness over flashy graphics or cinematics. My magazine needs to help people get the ideal jobs and roles they want, so I need to keep roles as accurate and realistic as possible. This research will allow me to better design my media product by telling me that I need to prioritize information and accuracy. This will allow me to better appeal to my audience and develop a successful media product.

title.rendered: Blog Post #6: Audience Theory Research – Audience Theories and Their Application to Media Products

content.rendered:
An audience is a group of people who are interested in or consume a specific type of content from a certain genre or person. Media producers need to understand their audiences in order to design successful media and appeal to them. Media companies like PBS Kids or NBC understand their audiences and design their production to adapt. PBS Kids’ audience includes children, so they invest in children’s television. NBC’s audience includes adults looking to be informed, so they display news content.

The Uses and Gratifications Theory suggests that audiences actively play a role in choosing what media they consume. If a consumer dislikes something, they will pick an alternative. People watch media for different reasons; they may consume something because it’s part of their identity, it’s entertaining, to be informed, to complete daily tasks, or to better connect with peers. A good example of this is Google Chrome. Chrome is a web browsing tool to complete common tasks online. It satisfied people because it allowed them to browse websites quickly. Media producers can learn that in order for their products to succeed. They need to either empower identities, entertain, inform, or provide to their audience.

Gauntlett’s Identity Theory states that audiences use media to help form their identities, and that identity is something that constantly changes, shaped by numerous factors. Audiences watch media that they enjoy to learn from; they begin to learn from role models and personality traits from which they experiment with. Representation is important since it allows more people to learn about personalities, causing variety in people. An example of a media group that appeals to an audience is K-Pop. K-Pop appeals to a global audience, with Koreans as a focus. It appeals to a lot of people by providing catchy pop music. Producers can use this theory to include a variety of perspectives in their content, causing people to relate to the media and thus increasing success.

Hall’s Reception Theory states that a media producer will embed their values in a piece of media, but allow the audience to interpret it based off their own beliefs and ideas. Preferred reading is when the audience interprets just how the original author intended. Negotiated reading is when the audience interprets the main core message but interprets other parts of the media differently because of their own world views. Oppositional reading is when the audience goes against the author’s original meaning and interprets it the opposite way.

A good example of this is the book “Animal Farm” by George Orwell. A commonly contested detail in the book is the fact that the pigs simplify the rules of the farm to a mantra: “two legs good, four legs bad” in order to teach the dumber animals the core ideas. Some believe that this is dangerous because it aggressively simplifies the rights and rules; others could believe it is justified because there is no practical way to communicate to dumber animals the rights they have. Audiences will interpret this as well as other details differently due to how detailed yet vague the book is.

I think Gauntlett’s Identity Theory makes the most sense. People (including me) have their personality formed based off the media we consume. Especially due to hyper-optimized algorithms in social media now, the media we receive is designed to feed into our own personality and preferences first beyond anything else. These theories help media producers understand their audiences and how exactly their media will be consumed, allowing them to optimize for maximum success and growth. I believe the Uses and Gratifications Theory will be most useful for me though, simply because trying to develop media that could be interpreted differently is difficult to do in something like a magazine versus a book.

title.rendered: Blog Post #4: An Analysis of How Magazine Genre Shape Content and Audience

content.rendered:
Gaming magazines are mainly focused on video games, specifically commentary on development, news from communities, and studios. The target audience is mainly composed of gamers, game developers, game designers, and people working at indie studios.

As seen above, the cover design of gaming magazines is focused on showing characters, highlights, and cinematic pictures from the latest popular video games. Color schemes usually include white, red, and black alongside the accent colors of the displayed game. The imagery usually includes vast scenes or prominent characters from a popular game. The headlines usually include the magazine’s brand name alongside a title or phrase mentioning a specific video game or a big question about PC specifications and game controversies. The language and tone are usually humorous, relatable and casual while showing mild frustration at problems within games or the industry. Featured topics often include big game releases, game updates, gaming hardware coverage, or fresh game leaks.

These visual conventions are effective at attracting readers, as they build up excitement and are visually appealing. Cinematic imagery from video games piques the interest of readers passing by, and flashy headlines covering big game releases, top games, or leaks build up a certain level of suspense and surprise, suspense that can only be resolved by looking at the magazine and displayed game or games. Red, white, and black colors alongside the subject games’ accent colors help introduce readers to the subject well while maintaining readability in normal paragraph texts. For example, this magazine shows Nintendo’s top 100 games, evoking a level of excitement into the reader. The diverse range of famous Nintendo IPs attracts readers’ attention by featuring their favorite characters.

As seen above, gaming magazines usually use dark, intense, and dangerous imagery. This is intentional, as it gives the magazines and featured games a level of “coolness”. People are attracted to them because they give off the impression of being serious, “epic”, and novel. This attracts and represents people who may have more mundane or boring lives; as intense activities that these people would be unable to do in real life, like fight in a war or navigate dangerous obstacles, are now activities that they can do with the click of a button.

The magazines shown above very much follow genre expectations. They all feature imagery of video games, contain red, black, and white color schemes, cover hardware or games, and oftentimes feature intense characteristics (like a sword or armor). These attract gamers with novel activities and interesting new content that keeps them hooked.
